KIDNAPPING SPREE

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A spate of kidnappings has gripped the South African Indian Muslim community– we investigate the modus operandi behind this growing crime trend.

Unique Selling Point:
HUGELY TOPICAL - NOT REALLY COVERED IN THE NEWS
WE HAVE A VICTIM
WE HAVE AUDIO RECORDINGS FROM KIDNAPPERS (LINKED TO OTHER CASES)
RE-ENACTMENTS WILL BE AWESOME



Summary:
In the last two years kidnappings for ransom have become an every day threat for the South African Indian community. There is currently an international syndicate and a string of opportunistic copy-cat groups terrorizing people demanding ransoms of as little as R70 000 up to R64 million.

We cast the spotlight the risks and the challenges behind this crime trend that seems to be spiralling out of control.

Further information:
We have seen South Africans of Indian origin being targeted as well as Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Chinease and Indian nationals. The reason? They often operate business that have access to large sums of cash.

There have been about 8 high profile kidnappings and at least one copy cat kidnapping a week in the last two years.

HISTORY
Kidnap for ransom is not a common South African crime trend. In countries like India, Pakistan and Mozambique – it is a ways of life.

With the influx of foreign nationals in SA, we are increasingly seeing the introduction of foreign crime trends.

WHO IS BEHIND IT
In Mozambique, we saw scores of kidnappings over a four-year period. Authorities eventually clamped down. Some kingpins were arrested and released on bail. They are now fugitives. It is suspected the same kingpins may be involved in some of the major kidnappings in South Africa.

While it appears highly organized syndicates are behind the big ransom kidnappings, there are also smaller or amateur groups carrying out “copy-cat” kidnappings – these are the worrying ones – they are extremely dangerous because of the inexperience. In the last six months two victims in copy-cat cases have been killed.

While some arrests have been made in the “copy-cat” incidents, other groups are continuing to kidnap especially business people.

CASES
• JANUARY 2018: the body of North West businessman Hasan Parvej (32) was found. He was kidnapped from his store some 70km from Mahikeng last week. The kidnappers demanded R1-million cash. The family only managed to raise some R70 000 and asked for more time. The kidnappers wanted the part payment and hours after the cash drop-off, Parvej’s body was found in bushes. He had multiple stab wounds.
• DECEMBER 2017: Over the holiday period, an Indian businessman, was kidnapped in Limpopo. The gang demanded R6-million cash. Police set-up a sting operation and arrested one suspect after a high-speed chase.
• AUGUST 2017: Pretoria businessman Omar Carrim (76) was released after being held captive for 137 days. It is believed the family was forced to pay a large ransom.
• 2017: Cape Town businessman Sadek Zhaun Ahmed was released after being kidnapped and held for several weeks. He also reportedly paid a large ransom.
• 2016: Businessman Naushad Deshmukh Khan (46) of Cape Town was kidnapped in late 2016 and held for weeks. He paid millions of rands in ransom and was freed.
• the Moosa family of Polokwane in 2016 after Anisah Moosa (36) was kidnapped. The gang demanded R3-million. The victim was freed after a shootout with police. Three men were later arrested. They were released on bail. One was shot dead in December in a robbery in Tzaneen

There have also been KZN cases – just confirming those details

WHAT IS THE MO WHEN THE HIT THE TARGET?
It is believed that the targets are kept under surveillance once they have been identified – their movements, their meetings, their habits are known to the kidnappers.

They will usually be taken while driving – they car will be boxed in and two men will take the victim, while a third will drive off with the victims car. The kidnappers are armed – usually with handguns and the ones doing the physical extraction usually wear gloves.

The cars are usually abandoned. In Carrim’s case – the R600k car was burnt – this is small change to the international syndicate.

In some cases, victims have been taken in broad daylight from their businesses.

HOW ARE THE VICTIMS KEPT?
• all of them are tied up – usually hands and feet
• they are beaten and abused in the first week to two weeks
• then the kidnappers usually ease up a bit, but with the constant threat of more beatings
• Carrim – was kept in a dark passages with his feet chained up for 137 days, but at times they would get his food that he wanted and even supplied him medication.

I WILL DO RE-ENACTMENTS TO TELL THESE ELEMENTS VISUALLY

WHO DO THEY CRIMINALS TARGET?
Weatlhy Indian, usually Muslim, Businessmen are targeted. They are considered soft targets that have access to large sums of cash because a lot of their businesses trade in cash.

The South African Indian Muslim Community also bands together and has a strong sense of community. In some cases – fellow businessmen have been known to all chip in to raise the cash ransom.

HOW MUCH RANSOM ARE WE TALKING?
Anything from as little as R50 000 to R64million.

The smaller copy-cat groups simply want cash in a box or a bag. They don’t have the resources to keep victims for months. These cases usually last between 24 -72 hours.

The internationally linked syndicates mean business. They want money paid in cash at international banks with family members having to fly to places like Dubai with millions of rands worth of money to deposit at a bank there.

These guys often don’t accept just one payment. In Carrim’s case they demanded a further big payment of over R10 million.

THE NEGOTIATIONS
I have recordings of the kidnappers calling the victims families to negotiate and give instructions. I am going to use it in the story. But will not be able to say which cases it is from because we don’t want to jeopardise the investigations.

THE TRAUMA DOESN’T END AFTER RELEASE
In a number of the highly profile cases they victim are released on condition that they continue to make interim payments to the kidnappers to ensure their safety. Should they speak out or stop payments the threat is that the kidnappers will come back for them, or their families.

The vicitms live in constant fear even after their release.

WHAT ARE THE COPS DOING?
Not nearly enough. The police hostage negotiators are world class. They have been trained internationally. BUT that’s where the expertise ends. The investigations fall flat because there of the usual police stories – cops are under resources and lack the expertise to hand these types of high level complex investigations.

To date, almost 4 months after Omar Carrim was released the police have not yet taken his statement.

UNDER REPORTED TO POLICE
Many kidnapping cases also go unreported. The families fear going to the police.
Local business people are seen as easy targets. The culprits involved in the major kidnappings have still not been brought to book.

THE VICTIMS ARE FEEDING THE KIDNAP FOR RANSOM TREND
- targets on our backs by paying
- makes the rest of community vulnerable
- not reporting prevents police intervention
- copy cats are easier to catch – could send message

CASE STUDY
Please understand that victims have been severely traumatised – no one is going to show their faces. The threats of being kidnapped again or their families being targeted is real. During my meetings with various players I have been asked if I am brave enough to take this on because of fear of retaliation – the international syndicate means business. I have personally approached three of the high profile vicitms who have all refused. A number of others have been approached on my behalf and have also declined.

BUT I have met with a Bangladeshi National that was kidnapped in 2016. He was beaten, they threatened to kill his family members and engaged with his mother in Bangladesh where he has property. He still lives in fear and is truly traumatised – I saw it in my interactions with him. He was kept for 16 days, drugged and given alcohol to disarm him. He was tied up, blind folded and beaten with a stick – he still bears the scars. He eventually escaped. We have reason to believe that he was one of the first victims in these copy-cat kidnappings – his story is relevant and gripping. HE WILL NOT SHOW HIS FACE, WE NEED TO ALTER HIS VOICE AND CHANGE HIS NAME. I completely respect this request having seen the fear in his eyes.

This is our only shot at getting a victim in the story.

EXPERTS
• DUDLEY BOOYSEN – KIDNAP & RANSOM SPECIALIST
He has worked in Iraq specializing in Kidnap & Ransom cases, and was part of the British Armed Forces for 10 years. He has indepth understanding of the phenomenon and the current SA threat. He offers close protection in SA and has seen an increased demand from Indian businessmen for protection – even an demand for bulletproof vehicles.
• DR GERARD LABUSCHAGNE – CRIMINAL PROFILER
He will be able to explain the psychology and the international crime trend expanding on the risks and challenges in the cases.
• SAPS
We explore what they are doing and NOT doing to bring these criminals to book and to get this crime trend under control.

Press Release:



Kidnapping Spree
Kidnapping wealthy business owners is fast becoming the latest money-making operation for brutal, crime syndicates who demand multi-million rand ransoms. While it appears highly organized syndicates are behind the big ransom kidnappings, there are also smaller or amateur groups carrying out “copy-cat” kidnappings. But as kidnappers become more daring and sophisticated, it gets increasingly difficult for police to make a breakthrough in any of the cases. Carte Blanche investigates the modus operandi behind a spate of kidnappings that has gripped the South African Muslim Indian community.


Script:


KIDNAP SPREE STRUCTURE

VO: Kidnappings for ransom is not a common South African crime trend - but in the last two years it has plagued the country and appears to be spiraling out of control.

The following audio clip is a kidnapper speaking to the family of a hostage.

KIDNAPPER: You listen when I talk. You keep talking I kill your brother. You involve the police your brother dies. My brother you try to be funny and he fucken dies.

LINK: These gangs mean business. They are armed. They are ruthless and they are making big money - demanding ransoms ranging from as little as R50 000 to over R50 million.

MARK: They understand that they have a commodity that they can make money on – and that is the victim.

KIDNAPPER: I am the one who took your brother // we are asking you give us R50 million in exchange of your brother. // We are a very power organisation. Do you understand?

VO: Kidnappings demanding massive ransoms are usually run by highly sophisticated syndicates. As an internationally accredited hostage negotiator, Mark Courtney is one of about 70 people in the world qualified to handle these cases.

MARK: // International crime is exactly that – it transcends all borders // INT3 M3// they have people who the snatch – they have people who do the holding and they have different people doing the negotiating and these three people may not be in the same city. INT3 M11

VO: Since December 2015 there has been at least 6 of these cases where over a 100 million rand has been paid in ransom.

• Meboob Valley Moosa was taken in KZN in 2015.
• Naushad Khan from Cape Town in 2016, and in the same year Anisah Moosa was taken from Polekwane.
• 2017 saw three high profile cases - Momad Imtiyaz Golam In KZN, Sadek Zhaun in Cape Town and Omar Carrim from Pretoria

LINK: It appears that the Indian Muslim Business Community is the prime target. The theory is that they have quick access to money as they often operate cash businesses and are believed to be soft targets.

VO: Courtney explains that with the influx of foreign nationals in SA, we are increasingly seeing the introduction of foreign crime trends.

MARK: Kidnapping is almost easy to do – they understand the community, they understand the culture of the community, they know that the community is to large degree unbanked // this is well known to the kidnappers and they go after these people because they know they have ready access to money.

KIDNAPPER: I am giving you 20 minutes to arrange R6 million – or else your brother dies.

VO: This is psychological warfare. Threats like these keep families from involving law enforcement says HAWKS investigator, Lt Col Andre Neethling.

NEETHLING: Fear is instilled in them. They are told that they will be killed if they involve law enforcement. // They are often told that they are in control of the police, that they control everything.

KIDNAPPER: You involve the police – I will know because the police are involved. Am I clear enough for you?
BROTHER: alright.
KIDNAPPER: You have 20 minutes to do what I told you or your brother dies.

VO: 70% of kidnapping cases are not reported – making it difficult for the police to get a grip on this scurge.

NEETHLING: // this is an absolutely new trend and we have to adapt our infiltration capacities // we need to find out who are these people. These people are sophisticated. // As much as the crime is evolving, the investigation is evolving with it.

VO: The police work closely with foreign intelligence and law enforcement agencies across a range of departments.

NEETHLING: We cannot always tell people exactly what we do // we have standard operating procedures in place that enables us to do an investigation an intervention in the background – absolutely in the background.

LINK: While it appears highly organized international syndicates are behind the big ransom kidnappings, there is a spike in “copy-cat” kidnappings run by smaller opportunistic groups – they are extremely dangerous because of the inexperience.

DUDLEY: The copy-cats just by themselves is a weekly occurrence.

VO: Dudley Booysen is a risk solutions consultant that is part of a network of investigators handling the kidnap & ransom cases in South Africa.

DUDLEY: the copy cats are just opportunists basically. // , they get the guy, they want to get the money as quick as possible without being compromised. // These guys should not be underestimated, they are known for extreme violence.

VO: A Bhangladeshi shop owner has agreed to share his story on the condition that we hide his identity. He was kidnapped two years ago by a copy-cat gang and still lives in fear.

JOHN: I thought they were going to kill me

VO: Four men came into his shop in Johannesburg armed with guns. He thought it was robbery.

JOHN: I was telling them whatever you want – just please take it. Mustn’t beat me, something like that. // They say no we didn’t come to rob the store. We come to take you. They point me gun, they, put me in the car.
MAC: Did you realise what was going on?
JOHN: I thought they came to kill me – not to kidnap // I didn’t know about kidnapping.

VO: He was held for 16 days and 16 nights in an unknown location, by the same crew that took him from his shop. Courtney says this is typical of copy cat gangs.

MARK: they are less professional – the teams are a lot smaller, // they can’t really run the operations – it’s too tight a budget.

VO: Because the gangs are small, there so much more that can go wrong in a copy-cat kidnapping.

In January this year Hasan Parvej was kidnapped from his shop in the North West. The kidnappers demanded R1-million in cash. But when the family could only come up with R70 000, the kidnappers wanted the money as a down payment.

Hours after the cash drop-off, Parvej’s body was found in bushes with multiple stab wounds.

Having secured the release of 54 people, Courtney says the killing of hostages is uncommon.

MARK: the reason why they kill the victims is because the victim recognises them. // they will keep you alive to give all the proof of life answers that are requested from the negotiating team and once the money has been transferred they will kill the victim.

VO: But even if you are fortunate enough to be kept alive – the circumstances are not ideal.

MAC: Did they give you food?
JOHN: Morning time that breakfast - they are beating me and dinner they are beating me. That’s my food – 16 days. // and they got weapon but they keep always next to him.

VO: This is the modus operandi used both by copy cat gangs and the pro’s, says Courtney.

MARK: The kidnappers beat them, starve them, sometimes torture them so that they are in the right mind set to communicate to their families to demand that their families pay ransoms – it is also then easier for the kidnappers to control that victim

JOHN: I was asking to them – why you beating me? Tell me? They say you don’t know? You earn money – that money belongs to me, it belongs to us. We want money – you kidnapped.

VO: The kidnappers contacted his mother in Bhangladesh, demanding a ransom of R500 000.

MAC: Did they get this money?
JOHN: Not a single cent. Because I am out of money. But after that there was another plan to use me to get information for another person.

VO: The kidnappers wanted to use him in their gang to sell out other potential targets to be kidnapped.

JOHN: So when I find out this is happening – I escape and I run away.

VO: Booysen says the fact that he was able to get out and escape without any ransom being paid shows just how amateur some of these copy-cat gangs are in comparison to the big syndicates.

DUDLEY: the international syndicates have a much better platform that they work from, we’re talking about surveillance, intelligence // they have that without the fear of being compromised – so they can keep the guys longer and they can ask for more ransom.

VO: The Omar Carrim kidnapping was run by professionals – they were in it for the long haul. He was taken in PRETORIA in AUGUST 2017.

DUDLEY: Mr Omar Carrim was kept for 137 days in a confined dark room.

VO: The kidnappers didn’t just abandon his luxury Mercedes Benz – it was burnt. Courtney says this is small change to international syndicates. While copy-cats gangs just want cash in a bag, the organised operators take a much more sophisticated approach.

MARK: We’re well aware that a lot of the ransoms paid in our community are paid off shore – using different methods of getting money whether it be physically carrying it out or transferring it through numerous banking institutions or unregulated banking as it were.

VO: One of these pseudo-banking systems is Hawala, used mostly in Arab countries. The system is based on trust - money is transferred via a network of hawala brokers. The sender gives the money to a broker, who then contacts another broker close to the receiver. The money is paid without any actual cash being moved – the transaction is quick and there is no record – making it difficult to trace says Lt Col Neethling.

NEETHLING: // it is quite easy to move money in those // pseudo banking process // it’s not a traditional matter where money is paid and here and transferred and there is a paper trial – it’s much more complicated than that.

VO: And the kidnappers are taking full advantage of unregulated systems according to Courtney.

MARK: When it comes to paying ransom – the payment doesn’t guarantee release – the payment doesn’t guarantee that it’s going to be the last payment. // you can maybe get what we call in the industry a double dip – where you get hit twice for a ransom
DUDLEY: even after the guy’s been released the kidnappers arrogance to say we still need a monthly payout from you guys or we’ll comeback for you or your family.

VO: Threats of further violence or even kidnappings are a reality. Listen as this Kidnapper spells it out to the son of a hostage.

KIDNAPPER: Also listen if you are playing game and your father is dying – still you are paying this money – you are not get the body, you will not see – but still you will pay this money – because we are watching you also.

VO: And without expert intervention, Courtney believes South Africans are at risk.

MARK: // when these get out of control, you can loose limbs, you can loose family members - // every time we deal with a kidnapping in an unprofessional manner we are making it easier for the kidnappers, we are making it easier for the copy cats because we are not tying them down.



 
PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: A spate of kidnappings has gripped the South African Indian Muslim community – with ransoms ranging from as little as R50 000 to over R50 million.

PROMO 2
VO: Kidnappers are terrorizing the South African Indian business community – demanding massive ransoms.

KIDNAPPER: I am the one who took your brother // I am giving you 20 minutes to arrange R6 million – or else your brother dies.

VO: We investigate this growing crime trend.

PROMO 3
VO: Ruthless gangs are kidnapping Indian businessmen – threatening their lives, beating them into submission and demanding huge ransons.

JOHN: I was asking to them – why you beating me? Tell me? They say you don’t know? // We want money – you kidnapped.

While it appears highly organized syndicates are behind the big ransom kidnappings, there are also smaller or amateur groups carrying out “copy-cat” kidnappings. But as kidnappers become more daring and sophisticated, it gets increasingly difficult for police to make a breakthrough in any of the cases. Carte Blanche investigates the modus operandi behind a spate of kidnappings that has gripped the South African Muslim Indian community. Script: KIDNAP SPREE STRUCTURE VO: Kidnappings for ransom is not a common South African crime trend - but in the last two years it has plagued the country and appears to be spiraling out of control. The following audio clip is a kidnapper speaking to the family of a hostage. KIDNAPPER: You listen when I talk. You keep talking I kill your brother. You involve the police your brother dies. My brother you try to be funny and he fucken dies. LINK: These gangs mean business. They are armed. They are ruthless and they are making big money - demanding ransoms ranging from as little as R50 000 to over R50 million. MARK: They understand that they have a commodity that they can make money on – and that is the victim. KIDNAPPER: I am the one who took your brother // we are asking you give us R50 million in exchange of your brother. // We are a very power organisation. Do you understand? VO: Kidnappings demanding massive ransoms are usually run by highly sophisticated syndicates. As an internationally accredited hostage negotiator, Mark Courtney is one of about 70 people in the world qualified to handle these cases. MARK: // International crime is exactly that – it transcends all borders // INT3 M3// they have people who the snatch – they have people who do the holding and they have different people doing the negotiating and these three people may not be in the same city. INT3 M11 VO: Since December 2015 there has been at least 6 of these cases where over a 100 million rand has been paid in ransom. • Meboob Valley Moosa was taken in KZN in 2015. • Naushad Khan from Cape Town in 2016, and in the same year Anisah Moosa was taken from Polekwane. • 2017 saw three high profile cases - Momad Imtiyaz Golam In KZN, Sadek Zhaun in Cape Town and Omar Carrim from Pretoria LINK: It appears that the Indian Muslim Business Community is the prime target. The theory is that they have quick access to money as they often operate cash businesses and are believed to be soft targets. VO: Courtney explains that with the influx of foreign nationals in SA, we are increasingly seeing the introduction of foreign crime trends. MARK: Kidnapping is almost easy to do – they understand the community, they understand the culture of the community, they know that the community is to large degree unbanked // this is well known to the kidnappers and they go after these people because they know they have ready access to money. KIDNAPPER: I am giving you 20 minutes to arrange R6 million – or else your brother dies. VO: This is psychological warfare. Threats like these keep families from involving law enforcement says HAWKS investigator, Lt Col Andre Neethling. NEETHLING: Fear is instilled in them. They are told that they will be killed if they involve law enforcement. // They are often told that they are in control of the police, that they control everything. KIDNAPPER: You involve the police – I will know because the police are involved. Am I clear enough for you? BROTHER: alright. KIDNAPPER: You have 20 minutes to do what I told you or your brother dies. VO: 70% of kidnapping cases are not reported – making it difficult for the police to get a grip on this scurge. NEETHLING: // this is an absolutely new trend and we have to adapt our infiltration capacities // we need to find out who are these people. These people are sophisticated. // As much as the crime is evolving, the investigation is evolving with it. VO: The police work closely with foreign intelligence and law enforcement agencies across a range of departments. NEETHLING: We cannot always tell people exactly what we do // we have standard operating procedures in place that enables us to do an investigation an intervention in the background – absolutely in the background. LINK: While it appears highly organized international syndicates are behind the big ransom kidnappings, there is a spike in “copy-cat” kidnappings run by smaller opportunistic groups – they are extremely dangerous because of the inexperience. DUDLEY: The copy-cats just by themselves is a weekly occurrence. VO: Dudley Booysen is a risk solutions consultant that is part of a network of investigators handling the kidnap & ransom cases in South Africa. DUDLEY: the copy cats are just opportunists basically. // , they get the guy, they want to get the money as quick as possible without being compromised. // These guys should not be underestimated, they are known for extreme violence. VO: A Bhangladeshi shop owner has agreed to share his story on the condition that we hide his identity. He was kidnapped two years ago by a copy-cat gang and still lives in fear. JOHN: I thought they were going to kill me VO: Four men came into his shop in Johannesburg armed with guns. He thought it was robbery. JOHN: I was telling them whatever you want – just please take it. Mustn’t beat me, something like that. // They say no we didn’t come to rob the store. We come to take you. They point me gun, they, put me in the car. MAC: Did you realise what was going on? JOHN: I thought they came to kill me – not to kidnap // I didn’t know about kidnapping. VO: He was held for 16 days and 16 nights in an unknown location, by the same crew that took him from his shop. Courtney says this is typical of copy cat gangs. MARK: they are less professional – the teams are a lot smaller, // they can’t really run the operations – it’s too tight a budget. VO: Because the gangs are small, there so much more that can go wrong in a copy-cat kidnapping. In January this year Hasan Parvej was kidnapped from his shop in the North West. The kidnappers demanded R1-million in cash. But when the family could only come up with R70 000, the kidnappers wanted the money as a down payment. Hours after the cash drop-off, Parvej’s body was found in bushes with multiple stab wounds. Having secured the release of 54 people, Courtney says the killing of hostages is uncommon. MARK: the reason why they kill the victims is because the victim recognises them. // they will keep you alive to give all the proof of life answers that are requested from the negotiating team and once the money has been transferred they will kill the victim. VO: But even if you are fortunate enough to be kept alive – the circumstances are not ideal. MAC: Did they give you food? JOHN: Morning time that breakfast - they are beating me and dinner they are beating me. That’s my food – 16 days. // and they got weapon but they keep always next to him. VO: This is the modus operandi used both by copy cat gangs and the pro’s, says Courtney. MARK: The kidnappers beat them, starve them, sometimes torture them so that they are in the right mind set to communicate to their families to demand that their families pay ransoms – it is also then easier for the kidnappers to control that victim JOHN: I was asking to them – why you beating me? Tell me? They say you don’t know? You earn money – that money belongs to me, it belongs to us. We want money – you kidnapped. VO: The kidnappers contacted his mother in Bhangladesh, demanding a ransom of R500 000. MAC: Did they get this money? JOHN: Not a single cent. Because I am out of money. But after that there was another plan to use me to get information for another person. VO: The kidnappers wanted to use him in their gang to sell out other potential targets to be kidnapped. JOHN: So when I find out this is happening – I escape and I run away. VO: Booysen says the fact that he was able to get out and escape without any ransom being paid shows just how amateur some of these copy-cat gangs are in comparison to the big syndicates. DUDLEY: the international syndicates have a much better platform that they work from, we’re talking about surveillance, intelligence // they have that without the fear of being compromised – so they can keep the guys longer and they can ask for more ransom. VO: The Omar Carrim kidnapping was run by professionals – they were in it for the long haul. He was taken in PRETORIA in AUGUST 2017. DUDLEY: Mr Omar Carrim was kept for 137 days in a confined dark room. VO: The kidnappers didn’t just abandon his luxury Mercedes Benz – it was burnt. Courtney says this is small change to international syndicates. While copy-cats gangs just want cash in a bag, the organised operators take a much more sophisticated approach. MARK: We’re well aware that a lot of the ransoms paid in our community are paid off shore – using different methods of getting money whether it be physically carrying it out or transferring it through numerous banking institutions or unregulated banking as it were. VO: One of these pseudo-banking systems is Hawala, used mostly in Arab countries. The system is based on trust - money is transferred via a network of hawala brokers. The sender gives the money to a broker, who then contacts another broker close to the receiver. The money is paid without any actual cash being moved – the transaction is quick and there is no record – making it difficult to trace says Lt Col Neethling. NEETHLING: // it is quite easy to move money in those // pseudo banking process // it’s not a traditional matter where money is paid and here and transferred and there is a paper trial – it’s much more complicated than that. VO: And the kidnappers are taking full advantage of unregulated systems according to Courtney. MARK: When it comes to paying ransom – the payment doesn’t guarantee release – the payment doesn’t guarantee that it’s going to be the last payment. // you can maybe get what we call in the industry a double dip – where you get hit twice for a ransom DUDLEY: even after the guy’s been released the kidnappers arrogance to say we still need a monthly payout from you guys or we’ll comeback for you or your family. VO: Threats of further violence or even kidnappings are a reality. Listen as this Kidnapper spells it out to the son of a hostage. KIDNAPPER: Also listen if you are playing game and your father is dying – still you are paying this money – you are not get the body, you will not see – but still you will pay this money – because we are watching you also. VO: And without expert intervention, Courtney believes South Africans are at risk. MARK: // when these get out of control, you can loose limbs, you can loose family members - // every time we deal with a kidnapping in an unprofessional manner we are making it easier for the kidnappers, we are making it easier for the copy cats because we are not tying them down. PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: A spate of kidnappings has gripped the South African Indian Muslim community – with ransoms ranging from as little as R50 000 to over R50 million. PROMO 2 VO: Kidnappers are terrorizing the South African Indian business community – demanding massive ransoms. KIDNAPPER: I am the one who took your brother // I am giving you 20 minutes to arrange R6 million – or else your brother dies. VO: We investigate this growing crime trend. PROMO 3 VO: Ruthless gangs are kidnapping Indian businessmen – threatening their lives, beating them into submission and demanding huge ransons. JOHN: I was asking to them – why you beating me? Tell me? They say you don’t know? // We want money – you kidnapped. metadata.Summary: In the last two years kidnappings for ransom have become an every day threat for the South African Indian community. There is currently an international syndicate and a string of opportunistic copy-cat groups terrorizing people demanding ransoms of as little as R70 000 up to R64 million. We cast the spotlight the risks and the challenges behind this crime trend that seems to be spiralling out of control.
metadata.Further information: We have seen South Africans of Indian origin being targeted as well as Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Chinease and Indian nationals. The reason? They often operate business that have access to large sums of cash. There have been about 8 high profile kidnappings and at least one copy cat kidnapping a week in the last two years. HISTORY Kidnap for ransom is not a common South African crime trend. In countries like India, Pakistan and Mozambique – it is a ways of life. With the influx of foreign nationals in SA, we are increasingly seeing the introduction of foreign crime trends. WHO IS BEHIND IT In Mozambique, we saw scores of kidnappings over a four-year period. Authorities eventually clamped down. Some kingpins were arrested and released on bail. They are now fugitives. It is suspected the same kingpins may be involved in some of the major kidnappings in South Africa. While it appears highly organized syndicates are behind the big ransom kidnappings, there are also smaller or amateur groups carrying out “copy-cat” kidnappings – these are the worrying ones – they are extremely dangerous because of the inexperience. In the last six months two victims in copy-cat cases have been killed. While some arrests have been made in the “copy-cat” incidents, other groups are continuing to kidnap especially business people. CASES • JANUARY 2018: the body of North West businessman Hasan Parvej (32) was found. He was kidnapped from his store some 70km from Mahikeng last week. The kidnappers demanded R1-million cash. The family only managed to raise some R70 000 and asked for more time. The kidnappers wanted the part payment and hours after the cash drop-off, Parvej’s body was found in bushes. He had multiple stab wounds. • DECEMBER 2017: Over the holiday period, an Indian businessman, was kidnapped in Limpopo. The gang demanded R6-million cash. Police set-up a sting operation and arrested one suspect after a high-speed chase. • AUGUST 2017: Pretoria businessman Omar Carrim (76) was released after being held captive for 137 days. It is believed the family was forced to pay a large ransom. • 2017: Cape Town businessman Sadek Zhaun Ahmed was released after being kidnapped and held for several weeks. He also reportedly paid a large ransom. • 2016: Businessman Naushad Deshmukh Khan (46) of Cape Town was kidnapped in late 2016 and held for weeks. He paid millions of rands in ransom and was freed. • the Moosa family of Polokwane in 2016 after Anisah Moosa (36) was kidnapped. The gang demanded R3-million. The victim was freed after a shootout with police. Three men were later arrested. They were released on bail. One was shot dead in December in a robbery in Tzaneen There have also been KZN cases – just confirming those details WHAT IS THE MO WHEN THE HIT THE TARGET? It is believed that the targets are kept under surveillance once they have been identified – their movements, their meetings, their habits are known to the kidnappers. They will usually be taken while driving – they car will be boxed in and two men will take the victim, while a third will drive off with the victims car. The kidnappers are armed – usually with handguns and the ones doing the physical extraction usually wear gloves. The cars are usually abandoned. In Carrim’s case – the R600k car was burnt – this is small change to the international syndicate. In some cases, victims have been taken in broad daylight from their businesses. HOW ARE THE VICTIMS KEPT? • all of them are tied up – usually hands and feet • they are beaten and abused in the first week to two weeks • then the kidnappers usually ease up a bit, but with the constant threat of more beatings • Carrim – was kept in a dark passages with his feet chained up for 137 days, but at times they would get his food that he wanted and even supplied him medication. I WILL DO RE-ENACTMENTS TO TELL THESE ELEMENTS VISUALLY WHO DO THEY CRIMINALS TARGET? Weatlhy Indian, usually Muslim, Businessmen are targeted. They are considered soft targets that have access to large sums of cash because a lot of their businesses trade in cash. The South African Indian Muslim Community also bands together and has a strong sense of community. In some cases – fellow businessmen have been known to all chip in to raise the cash ransom. HOW MUCH RANSOM ARE WE TALKING? Anything from as little as R50 000 to R64million. The smaller copy-cat groups simply want cash in a box or a bag. They don’t have the resources to keep victims for months. These cases usually last between 24 -72 hours. The internationally linked syndicates mean business. They want money paid in cash at international banks with family members having to fly to places like Dubai with millions of rands worth of money to deposit at a bank there. These guys often don’t accept just one payment. In Carrim’s case they demanded a further big payment of over R10 million. THE NEGOTIATIONS I have recordings of the kidnappers calling the victims families to negotiate and give instructions. I am going to use it in the story. But will not be able to say which cases it is from because we don’t want to jeopardise the investigations. THE TRAUMA DOESN’T END AFTER RELEASE In a number of the highly profile cases they victim are released on condition that they continue to make interim payments to the kidnappers to ensure their safety. Should they speak out or stop payments the threat is that the kidnappers will come back for them, or their families. The vicitms live in constant fear even after their release. WHAT ARE THE COPS DOING? Not nearly enough. The police hostage negotiators are world class. They have been trained internationally. BUT that’s where the expertise ends. The investigations fall flat because there of the usual police stories – cops are under resources and lack the expertise to hand these types of high level complex investigations. To date, almost 4 months after Omar Carrim was released the police have not yet taken his statement. UNDER REPORTED TO POLICE Many kidnapping cases also go unreported. The families fear going to the police. Local business people are seen as easy targets. The culprits involved in the major kidnappings have still not been brought to book. THE VICTIMS ARE FEEDING THE KIDNAP FOR RANSOM TREND - targets on our backs by paying - makes the rest of community vulnerable - not reporting prevents police intervention - copy cats are easier to catch – could send message CASE STUDY Please understand that victims have been severely traumatised – no one is going to show their faces. The threats of being kidnapped again or their families being targeted is real. During my meetings with various players I have been asked if I am brave enough to take this on because of fear of retaliation – the international syndicate means business. I have personally approached three of the high profile vicitms who have all refused. A number of others have been approached on my behalf and have also declined. BUT I have met with a Bangladeshi National that was kidnapped in 2016. He was beaten, they threatened to kill his family members and engaged with his mother in Bangladesh where he has property. He still lives in fear and is truly traumatised – I saw it in my interactions with him. He was kept for 16 days, drugged and given alcohol to disarm him. He was tied up, blind folded and beaten with a stick – he still bears the scars. He eventually escaped. We have reason to believe that he was one of the first victims in these copy-cat kidnappings – his story is relevant and gripping. HE WILL NOT SHOW HIS FACE, WE NEED TO ALTER HIS VOICE AND CHANGE HIS NAME. I completely respect this request having seen the fear in his eyes. This is our only shot at getting a victim in the story. EXPERTS • DUDLEY BOOYSEN – KIDNAP & RANSOM SPECIALIST He has worked in Iraq specializing in Kidnap & Ransom cases, and was part of the British Armed Forces for 10 years. He has indepth understanding of the phenomenon and the current SA threat. He offers close protection in SA and has seen an increased demand from Indian businessmen for protection – even an demand for bulletproof vehicles. • DR GERARD LABUSCHAGNE – CRIMINAL PROFILER He will be able to explain the psychology and the international crime trend expanding on the risks and challenges in the cases. • SAPS We explore what they are doing and NOT doing to bring these criminals to book and to get this crime trend under control.
